chapter_note.about: Cross-validation answers one question: how will this model do on data it has never seen? You hide part of the training data, train on the rest and score on the hidden part. Then you rotate which part is hidden and average. The same scores let you choose settings such as k or λ without touching the test set. The exam asks you to count splits and fits, compute the CV error from fold errors, and judge protocols for imbalanced data and leakage.

chapter_note.simple: Cross-validation is a fair way to test a model using only the data you already have. You cut the data into pieces. You hide one piece, learn from the others and test on the hidden piece. Then you hide the next piece and repeat. Averaging the test scores tells you how the model will behave on new data, and it also lets you choose the best settings. The real test set stays sealed until the end. Careful habits, such as keeping the class mix and fitting every adjustment inside each round, stop the score from being too good to be true.

cards.title: Purpose of cross-validation
cards.simple: You are preparing for a big exam and you have 5 old papers. If you study all 5 and then test yourself on the same 5, you will score well, but that proves nothing about the real exam. So you hide one paper, study the other 4, and test yourself on the hidden one. Then you hide a different paper and repeat. The average of those scores is an honest guess for the real exam. You also use these scores to decide how to study. The real exam (the test set) stays sealed until the very end. In exam words: cross-validation estimates generalisation error and tunes hyperparameters without touching the test set.
cards.idea: A model's error on its own training data is too rosy, because the model has already seen the answers. **Cross-validation (CV)** gives a fairer number. It repeatedly hides part of the training pool, trains on the rest, and scores the model on the hidden part. The average score estimates how the model will do on new data. You use it to choose settings called **hyperparameters**, and you keep the test set sealed until the end.
cards.definition:
$$\text{CV estimate}=\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}\text{error on held-out part } i$$

Symbols: the data is split into a **training pool** (used for fitting and tuning) and a **test set** (opened once, at the end). A **hyperparameter** is a setting chosen before training, such as $k$ in k-NN or $\lambda$ in ridge. The part hidden in each round is the validation fold.
cards.intuition_full: Training error answers 'how well does the model remember what it saw?' That is rarely what you want. You want to know how it does on data it has never seen. A hidden part imitates new data, because the model never trained on it. One hidden part can be unlucky, so CV rotates which part is hidden and averages. That is why CV is steadier than a single split. There is a second job. To pick between models you need scores you can compare fairly. If you use the test set for picking, the test set stops being new data, because you have tuned to it. That is why the test set is opened once, after every choice has been made. Think of three roles: training data to learn, validation data to choose, test data to report.

example.setup: You have 100 labelled samples. 20 go into a sealed test set. Three models A, B and C are tuned on the other 80 (the training pool). Training errors are A 0%, B 6%, C 12%. Cross-validation errors on held-out parts are A 31%, B 14%, C 19%. Which model do you choose, and when do you open the test set?
steps: Split first: 80 samples in the training pool and 20 in the test set. The test set is sealed.
Training errors: A 0%, B 6%, C 12%. A looks best, but a model can score 0% by memorising.
CV errors on held-out parts: A 31%, B 14%, C 19%. Now A is the worst.
Choose by CV error. B is the lowest at 14%.
Open the test set once, for B only. Suppose B scores 15%. Report 15%, which is close to the CV estimate of 14%.
example.answer: Choose B. Report its single test-set error (15%).

examples.setup: Model X has training error 2% and CV error 25%. Model Y has training error 12% and CV error 14%. After the choice is made, the sealed test set gives 24% for X and 15% for Y. examples.setup: Models P and Q are scored with 5 folds of 20 samples each. Mistakes per fold: P makes 3, 5, 4, 6, 2. Q makes 5, 2, 4, 3, 4. Someone judges using fold 1 only. What does fold 1 say, and what does the full CV say?
steps: Fold 1 alone: P makes 3 mistakes (15%) and Q makes 5 (25%). It says P is better.
All folds: P makes 3 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 20 mistakes. Q makes 5 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 18.
Out of 100 predictions, P errs 20% and Q errs 18%.
The ranking flipped. One lucky split misled; averaging over folds gives a steadier verdict.
examples.answer: Fold 1 says P. The full CV says Q (18% against 20%). One split is not enough.

how: Set the test set aside first and leave it alone until the end.
Split the remaining pool into folds.
In each round, train on some folds and score on the held-out fold.
Average the scores. Choose the model or setting with the best average.
Refit on the whole pool, then use the test set once to report the final number.
cards.mistake: Using the training error, or the test set, to choose a model. Training error rewards memorising. Using the test set again and again turns it into a second validation set, and the final score is then too optimistic.
edge_cases: Very small datasets: each held-out part is tiny, so the CV score is noisy.
Time-ordered data: random folds let the future leak into the past. Use ordered splits instead.
Huge datasets: one validation split can be enough, since it is already large.

cards.title: k-fold mechanics
cards.simple: Think of dealing a pack of cards into 4 piles of 3. In round 1, pile 1 is the quiz and piles 2, 3 and 4 are the study material. In round 2, pile 2 is the quiz and the other three are the study material. You carry on like that. After 4 rounds every card has been in a quiz pile exactly once, and in the study material three times. Nothing is wasted, and nothing is quizzed on something it has just studied. In exam words: k-fold CV splits the data into k folds, validates on each fold once and trains on the other k − 1.
cards.idea: In **k-fold cross-validation** you split the data into k equal folds. In each round, one fold is the validation fold and the other k − 1 folds are the training set. After k rounds every sample has been validated exactly once. Each round trains on $\frac{k-1}{k}$ of the data.
cards.definition:
$$\text{fold size}=\frac nk,\qquad \text{training size per round}=n\cdot\frac{k-1}{k}$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of samples in the pool and $k$ is the number of folds. Each sample is validated once and used for training $k-1$ times. The $k$ validation folds never overlap. The $k$ training sets do overlap.
cards.intuition_full: The folds partition the data: they cover everything and do not overlap. That gives two guarantees. First, every sample is validated once, so none is wasted and none is favoured. Second, a model is never scored on a sample it trained on in the same round. A larger k means a bigger training set in each round, closer to the full data, so each model looks more like the final model. It also means more rounds, so more work. Check the small cases. With k = 2 each round trains on half the data. With k = n each round trains on all but one sample.

example.setup: Twelve samples, numbered 1 to 12, are dealt into k = 4 folds in order: fold 1 is samples 1 to 3, fold 2 is 4 to 6, fold 3 is 7 to 9, fold 4 is 10 to 12. Write down the 4 rounds. How often is each sample validated, and how often does it train?
steps: Fold size = 12 / 4 = 3. Training size per round = 12 − 3 = 9.
Round 1: validate on samples 1 to 3, train on 4 to 12.
Round 2: validate on 4 to 6, train on 1 to 3 and 7 to 12.
Round 3: validate on 7 to 9, train on the other 9 samples.
Round 4: validate on 10 to 12, train on 1 to 9.
Look down any column: exactly one V and three T. Each sample is validated once and trains 3 = k − 1 times.
example.answer: Each round trains on 9 and validates on 3. Every sample is validated once and trains in the other 3 rounds.

cards.title: CV error estimate
cards.simple: Say you take 5 mock tests and make 12, 8, 10, 14 and 6 mistakes. To say how good you are, you do not quote your best day or your worst day. You take the average: 50 mistakes over 5 tests is 10 per test. Cross-validation does exactly this with the error from each fold. If the tests have different numbers of questions, a longer test should count for more, so you add up all the mistakes and divide by all the questions. In exam words: the CV error is the mean of the fold errors, weighted by fold size when the folds are unequal.
cards.idea: Each round of CV gives one error number from its validation fold. The **CV estimate** is the average of these numbers. If all folds have the same size, take the plain mean. If the sizes differ, weight each fold by its size. That works out to total mistakes divided by total samples.
cards.definition:
$$\widehat{E}_{CV}=\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}E_i\qquad\text{(equal folds)}$$

$$\widehat{E}_{CV}=\frac{\sum_i n_iE_i}{\sum_i n_i}=\frac{\text{total mistakes}}{\text{total samples}}\qquad\text{(unequal folds)}$$

Symbols: $E_i$ is the error rate on fold $i$ and $n_i$ is the size of fold $i$.
cards.intuition_full: A fold with more samples gives a more reliable error rate, so it deserves a bigger say. Weighting by size gives exactly total mistakes over total samples, so every validation prediction counts once. If you average the rates of unequal folds, a tiny fold gets the same say as a huge one, and the result is distorted. The mean also hides how much the folds disagree. Two models with the same mean can differ in spread, and the one with steadier fold errors is easier to trust. Never report only the best fold. It is the most flattering of k numbers, and it does not estimate anything.

example.setup: 5-fold CV with equal folds gives error rates of 12%, 8%, 10%, 14% and 6%. What is the CV estimate?
steps: Add the fold errors: 12 + 8 + 10 + 14 + 6 = 50.
Divide by the number of folds: 50 / 5 = 10.
Not the best fold (6%) and not the worst fold (14%). The estimate uses all five.

examples.answer: Both means are 10, but A's estimate is more trustworthy because its folds agree.

cards.title: Leave-one-out
cards.simple: Leave-one-out is the most extreme way of hiding data. With 5 friends, you hide one friend, guess his answer using the other four, then hide the next friend, and so on. Five friends means five rounds, and in each round you learn from almost everyone: 4 out of 5. This is a very fair test, but you do the whole job 5 times. With a million friends it would take a million rounds. In exam words: leave-one-out CV uses k = n. It trains n models, each on n − 1 samples.
cards.idea: **Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)** is k-fold with k = n. Each round hides exactly one sample, trains on the other n − 1, and tests on the hidden one. After n rounds you have n predictions, and the error is the fraction that were wrong (or the average squared error).
cards.definition:
$$\text{LOOCV}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}L\!\left(y_i,\ \hat f^{(-i)}(x_i)\right)$$

Symbols: $\hat f^{(-i)}$ is the model trained on every sample except sample $i$, and $L$ is the loss, such as 0-1 error or squared error. It needs $n$ fits, each on $n-1$ samples. There is no randomness in the folds.
cards.intuition_full: Each round's model has seen all but one sample, so it is almost the full model. That makes the estimate very close to the error of the model trained on everything: low bias. The price is cost, because you fit n models. The rounds are also nearly the same model repeated, so their errors move together. For some models the n fits can be avoided: for 1-NN you only need the nearest other point, and for least squares there is a shortcut using leverage. When doing 1-NN by hand, remember to leave the held-out point out of its own neighbour search. Otherwise it finds itself at distance 0, and the error collapses to the training error.

example.setup: Five points on a line: x = 1, 3, 4, 8, 9 with labels A, B, A, B, B. Use the 1-nearest-neighbour rule (the nearest OTHER point) with leave-one-out CV. What is the LOOCV error rate?
steps: 5 points means 5 rounds. Each round hides one point and predicts it from the nearest of the other four.
Hide x = 1 (A): the nearest other point is x = 3 (B, distance 2). Predict B. Wrong.
Hide x = 3 (B): the nearest is x = 4 (A, distance 1). Predict A. Wrong.
Hide x = 4 (A): the nearest is x = 3 (B, distance 1). Predict B. Wrong.

cards.title: Counting splits and fits
cards.simple: Count the work like a teacher marking practice papers. First lock the papers for the final exam in a drawer, because they are not part of the practice. Hiding one paper at a time over 320 papers makes 320 rounds. If you try 6 study plans and check each on 5 groups of papers, that is 6 × 5 = 30 rounds. At the end you study once more with the best plan on all the papers, so 31. In exam words: remove the test data first; LOOCV splits = pool size; fits = grid size × k, plus 1 refit.
cards.idea: Counting questions all follow one order. First **remove the test set**. What is left is the pool. LOOCV makes one split per pool sample. K-fold makes k splits. Searching a grid of G settings with k folds trains $G\times k$ models, and the final refit on the whole pool adds 1.
cards.definition:
$$\text{pool}=N-N_{test},\qquad \text{LOOCV splits}=\text{pool},\qquad \text{grid fits}=G\cdot k\ (+1\text{ refit})$$

Symbols: $N$ is the total number of samples, $N_{test}$ the samples kept for testing, $G$ the number of hyperparameter combinations and $k$ the number of folds. Two hyperparameters multiply: $G=G_1\times G_2$.
cards.intuition_full: Follow the order of events. The test set is set aside before anything else, so it can never appear in a CV count. A split is one round of 'train here, validate there'. K-fold has k of them. LOOCV has one per pool sample. If you repeat the whole CV for every candidate setting, you multiply by the number of candidates. After choosing the winner you usually train one final model on the whole pool, and that is the +1. Irrelevant numbers such as the number of classes or features never change a count. The other common question is the training size per round, which is pool × (k − 1)/k.

example.setup: A dataset has 400 samples. 80 are kept for testing. On the remaining pool: (a) How many LOOCV splits are there? steps: The CV pool is 400 − 80 = 320 samples. The test set is never counted.
(a) LOOCV makes one split per pool sample: 320 splits.
(b) 5-fold: validation = 320 / 5 = 64 and training = 320 − 64 = 256.
(c) 6 values × 5 folds = 30 fits.
Add the final refit on the whole pool: 30 + 1 = 31 fits.

cards.title: Bias, variance and cost of CV
cards.simple: Imagine judging a cook by letting them use only half the ingredients. Their dish tastes worse than it would with everything, so you underrate the cook. If you give them almost all the ingredients, your judgement is fairer. That is the bias of the CV score: less data in each round means a weaker model and a gloomier score. But giving almost everything means redoing the dish once per ingredient, which is slow, and the dishes come out nearly identical, so the rounds are not independent opinions. In exam words: a larger k gives lower bias but higher cost; LOOCV has the lowest bias, but its n models are highly correlated.
cards.idea: The choice of k is a trade. A small k trains on less data, so each model is weaker and the CV error is **too pessimistic** (biased high). A large k trains on almost all the data, so the bias is small, but you fit **more models**, and those models are nearly copies of each other. k = 5 or 10 is the usual compromise.
cards.definition:
$$\text{training size}=n\,\frac{k-1}{k},\qquad \text{fits}=k,\qquad \text{work}\approx n(k-1)\ \ (\text{if training time}\propto\text{size})$$

Symbols: $n$ is the pool size and $k$ the number of folds. Smaller training sets give a pessimistic estimate, which is the bias. LOOCV has $k=n$ and the smallest bias. Two LOOCV training sets share $n-2$ of their $n-1$ samples, so the models are nearly identical.
cards.intuition_full: Bias here means: does the CV error differ from the error of the model you will really deploy, trained on all n samples? A model trained on fewer samples is worse (that is what a learning curve shows), so a small-k estimate lands above the truth. As k grows the gap closes. The variance of the estimate is subtler. The k errors you average come from overlapping training sets, so they are positively correlated, and averaging correlated numbers helps less than averaging independent ones. LOOCV is the extreme case because its models are almost identical. That is why LOOCV, despite its low bias, is not always the lowest-variance choice. 5 or 10 is the safe middle.

example.setup: A pool has n = 200 samples. Compare k = 2, 5, 10 and 200 (LOOCV). Find the training size per round, the number of fits, and the total work relative to one fit on all 200 samples, if training time is proportional to training size.
steps: Training size = 200 × (k − 1)/k. For k = 2 it is 100. For k = 5 it is 160. For k = 10 it is 180. For k = 200 it is 199.
A training set smaller than 200 gives a weaker model and a pessimistic score. The shortfall is 100, 40, 20 and 1 samples.
Number of fits = k: 2, 5, 10 and 200.
Work relative to one full fit = k × (training size) / 200 = k − 1. That is 1, 4, 9 and 199.
k = 5 or 10 keeps the bias small for modest work. LOOCV has the least bias but costs 199 times as much.

cards.title: Stratified folds
cards.simple: Imagine a class of 100 students where only 10 wear glasses. If you make 5 teams by picking at random, one team might get no glasses wearers at all. You cannot test a 'spot the glasses' method on a team that has none. Stratified teams fix this. You deliberately put 2 glasses wearers in every team, so each team looks like the whole class in miniature. In exam words: stratified k-fold keeps the class ratio the same in every fold. Use it for imbalanced data.
cards.idea: In plain k-fold the folds are random. With a rare class, a fold can get too many of it, or none. **Stratified k-fold** deals out each class separately, so every fold has the same share of each class as the whole data. For imbalanced data it is the safe default, and you should report a metric that sees the rare class, such as AUC or recall, not plain accuracy.
cards.definition:
For a class with $n_c$ samples, stratified $k$-fold puts about $n_c/k$ of them in each fold.

$$\text{positives per fold}\approx\frac{n_{pos}}{k}$$

Symbols: $n_{pos}$ is the number of positive samples and $k$ the number of folds. The same rule holds for every class. Stratify on the labels, not on the features.
cards.intuition_full: A rare class makes plain random folds unreliable. If 10 of 100 samples are positive and you make 5 random folds, the positives could split 4, 0, 3, 1, 2. The fold with 0 positives cannot measure recall at all, because recall divides by the number of positives. The fold with 4 is twice as positive as average. Each fold's score then reflects the luck of the split, and the average is noisy. Stratification removes that luck: 2 positives in each fold, always. Accuracy has its own trap on imbalanced data. A model that always says 'negative' gets 90% accuracy when 10% are positive, and finds nothing. AUC and recall do not have this problem.

example.setup: A dataset has 100 samples: 10 positive and 90 negative. It is split into 5 folds of 20. Random folds contain 4, 0, 3, 1 and 2 positives. Compare them with stratified folds, using an 'always negative' model's accuracy in each fold.
steps: Overall positive rate: 10 / 100 = 10%.
Random folds: positives per fold are 4, 0, 3, 1, 2 (total 10). Fold 2 has none, so recall cannot even be computed there. Fold 1 has 20% positives.
Stratified folds: 10 / 5 = 2 positives and 90 / 5 = 18 negatives in every fold of 20. Every fold is 10% positive.
'Always negative' accuracy = 1 − (positives / 20). Random folds: 80%, 100%, 85%, 95%, 90%. Stratified: 90% in every fold.
The averages agree (90%), but random folds swing by 20 points. Stratified folds do not.
example.answer: Stratified folds put 2 positives and 18 negatives in every fold. Random folds can leave a fold with no positives.

cards.what: In plain k-fold the folds are random. With a rare class, a fold can get too many of it, or none. **Stratified k-fold** deals out each class separately, so every fold has the same share of each class as the whole data. For imbalanced data it is the safe default, and you should report a metric that sees the rare class, such as AUC or recall, not plain accuracy.
cards.what_full:
In plain k-fold the folds are random. With a rare class, a fold can get too many of it, or none. **Stratified k-fold** deals out each class separately, so every fold has the same share of each class as the whole data. For imbalanced data it is the safe default, and you should report a metric that sees the rare class, such as AUC or recall, not plain accuracy.

For a class with $n_c$ samples, stratified $k$-fold puts about $n_c/k$ of them in each fold.

$$\text{positives per fold}\approx\frac{n_{pos}}{k}$$

Symbols: $n_{pos}$ is the number of positive samples and $k$ the number of folds. The same rule holds for every class. Stratify on the labels, not on the features.

**Worked example.** A dataset has 100 samples: 10 positive and 90 negative. It is split into 5 folds of 20. Random folds contain 4, 0, 3, 1 and 2 positives. Compare them with stratified folds, using an 'always negative' model's accuracy in each fold.

1. Overall positive rate: 10 / 100 = 10%.
2. Random folds: positives per fold are 4, 0, 3, 1, 2 (total 10). Fold 2 has none, so recall cannot even be computed there. Fold 1 has 20% positives.
3. Stratified folds: 10 / 5 = 2 positives and 90 / 5 = 18 negatives in every fold of 20. Every fold is 10% positive.
4. 'Always negative' accuracy = 1 − (positives / 20). Random folds: 80%, 100%, 85%, 95%, 90%. Stratified: 90% in every fold.
5. The averages agree (90%), but random folds swing by 20 points. Stratified folds do not.

**Answer:** Stratified folds put 2 positives and 18 negatives in every fold. Random folds can leave a fold with no positives.

**Check yourself:** 120 samples, 24 positive, 6 stratified folds. How many positives are in each fold?

*Answer:* 24 / 6 = 4 positives in each fold of 20.

cards.title: Data leakage
cards.simple: Imagine you study for a quiz and, by accident, you read the answer key. Your score is great, but it says nothing about how much you learned. Data leakage is the same thing. If anything about the quiz questions (the validation fold) shapes how you prepare, the score comes out too good. A common slip is to work out averages for rescaling, or to pick the best features, using all the data before cross-validation. Those numbers already contain a peek at the validation data. Do every preparation step inside each round, using only that round's training part. In exam words: fit scalers and feature selectors inside the fold.
cards.idea: **Leakage** means information from the validation data sneaks into training. Any step that learns from data (a scaler's mean and standard deviation, feature selection, imputation values, PCA) must be fitted on the training part of each fold only, and then applied to the validation part. Fitting it on all the data first makes the CV score **too optimistic**.
cards.definition:
For each CV round:

1. Fit the preprocessing (scaler, selector, imputer) on the training part only.
2. Apply those fitted numbers to both the training part and the validation part.
3. Train the model.
4. Score on the validation part.

The leaky version fits the preprocessing on all the data before splitting. The same rule holds for the test set: fit on the pool, then apply to the test set.
cards.intuition_full: The validation fold is supposed to play the role of data the model has never seen. A mean computed on all the data includes the validation rows, so the training pipeline has already 'seen' them. Here is a small example. If the validation point is an outlier, the mean of all the data is dragged toward it. Centring with that mean makes the outlier look less extreme than it really is. In a real deployment the new data would not have helped compute the mean, so the honest number is the training-only mean. Feature selection with labels is even worse: choosing the features that best predict the labels, using all labels, builds the answer into the model. The score looks great, and it falls apart on genuinely new data. Duplicate rows in different folds leak in the same way.

example.setup: A feature has values 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 in the training part and 35 in the validation part. Centre it by subtracting the mean. Compare the mean computed from the training part only with the mean computed on all six values. What is the centred validation value in each case?
steps: The data: training values 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and one validation value 35.
Honest mean, training only: (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9) / 5 = 25 / 5 = 5.
Leaky mean, all six values: (25 + 35) / 6 = 60 / 6 = 10.
The leaky mean moved from 5 to 10, pulled toward the validation point.
Centred validation value: honest 35 − 5 = 30, leaky 35 − 10 = 25. The leak makes the outlier look less extreme.
example.answer: Honest mean 5 gives 30. The leaky mean 10 gives 25. The validation point has shaped its own preprocessing.

examples.setup: A hospital dataset has 100 rows from 50 patients, two rows per patient (almost the same measurements). It is split into 5 random folds of 20. On average, how many of the 20 validation rows have their twin in the training part?
steps: Take one validation row. Its twin is one of the other 99 rows.
19 of those 99 rows are in the same validation fold. The other 80 are in the training part.
Chance the twin is in the training part: 80 / 99 ≈ 0.81.
Out of 20 validation rows: 20 × 80 / 99 ≈ 16.2 on average.
So about 16 rows are 'seen' in training through their twin. The fix is group k-fold: keep both rows of a patient in the same fold.
examples.answer: About 16 of 20. Duplicates leak, so keep each patient's rows together.

cards.title: Model selection
cards.simple: You are choosing between 4 study plans. For each plan you take 4 practice tests and note the mistakes. You do not pick the plan with the single best day. You average each plan's 4 scores and choose the plan with the lowest average. Then you study once more with that plan, using all your practice papers, and take the real exam once. Remember that the best average you saw is a bit lucky, because you picked the best of several. So quote the real exam score, not the practice average. In exam words: choose the hyperparameter with the lowest mean CV error, refit on the full pool, and report the test error once.
cards.idea: To choose a hyperparameter (k in k-NN, λ in ridge, tree depth), compute the CV error for every candidate and pick the lowest **mean**. Then refit on the whole pool with that value. The CV score of the winner is slightly optimistic, because it is the best of several noisy numbers. The honest final number comes from the test set, used once.
cards.definition:
$$\hat h=\arg\min_{h}\ \widehat{E}_{CV}(h)$$

Then refit on the whole pool with $\hat h$ and report the error on the test set.

Symbols: $h$ is a candidate value of the hyperparameter, $\widehat{E}_{CV}(h)$ is its mean CV error, and argmin means 'the value of $h$ with the smallest score'.
cards.intuition_full: Choosing is a competition between candidates, each scored on the same folds. The mean is the right summary, because it uses every fold, so one lucky fold cannot win alone. Picking the minimum of several noisy scores biases the winner's score downward. Suppose 40 settings are all equally good. The best of 40 noisy scores will look better than any of them really is. So the CV score of the winner is optimistic, and you use the test set, which took no part in the choice, to report. After picking, you refit on the whole pool. That is more data than any single round had, so the final model is better. Nested CV (an outer loop for reporting and an inner loop for tuning) does the same job when you cannot spare a test set.
